claims.text: A defect- and oxygen-inclusive DFT+CPA and machine-learning model will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical approaches over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr material is bulk and polycrystalline and is produced by standard casting.
Cast HfNbTaTiZr naturally contains atomic-scale chemical disorder.
Measurements exist for an HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
DFT+CPA can capture chemical disorder and oxygen interstitial effects in HfNbTaTiZr.
Machine-learning calibration to experimental data can account for nonideal atomic configurations beyond the DFT+CPA description.
Point defects and oxygen precipitates make explicit contributions to electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Impurity and defect scattering dominates over phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr from 0 to 200 K.
Phonon contributions become significant in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Atomic-scale substitutional disorder, point defects, and oxygen interstitials modify electron scattering and effective electronic relaxation times.
Explicitly representing defects and oxygen changes the calculated electron mean free path and relaxation time relative to an ideal crystal.
Defect-induced electron scattering increases resistivity or moderates conductivity, with the effect especially pronounced at low temperature.
A transport calculation has quantitatively reproduced nonlinear electrical resistivity and thermopower over 2–400 K for chemically and topologically disordered HEA and metallic-glass samples.
The defect-inclusive model will predict lower cryogenic conductivity than a perfect-crystal model.
The defect-inclusive model will predict a more gradual conductivity decline and moderated temperature dependence over 300–1200 K.
The model will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–20% relative to analytical models that ignore defects.
The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with or without 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Samples with substantially different impurity types or concentrations and temperatures outside the specified intervals may require model refinement.
Prior literature recommends studying oxygen contamination and its relationship to disorder parameters in refractory complex concentrated alloys and refractory high-entropy alloys.
A deviation greater than ±15% at any specified temperature, or failure to observe the predicted temperature trend, will falsify the model hypothesis.
